In response to the question on support for children of parents who are in prison, I'd like to say that the children of parents who are incarcerated must not be forced to cut links with their parents. Therefore, we have three principles guiding our work: the protection of family ties, psychological support of the child, and not permitting the child stigmatization. The fact of the parents being being deprived of liberty does not automatically curtail the parental rights. If that is in the best interest of the child, then contact with the parents remains possible through visits, through telephone calls and other forms of contact foreseen by law. If one of the parents is in a place of deprivation of liberty, the child, as a rule, continues to live with their second parent or with relatives. If both parents are unable to care for the child, then the state bodies place the children in, first and foremost, a family environment through guardianship or custodianship. In 2025, there were 93 such children. Particular attention is given to the psychological state of these children. In Kazakhstan, we have centres for psychological support, and in schools, there are diagnoses that are provided and psychological support is provided. This makes it possible to detect any alarm or when a child is experiencing difficulty and to provide the child with support accordingly. The fact that a parent is deprived of their liberty should not per se be disclosed in the educational environment, and it cannot serve as a basis for any form of discrimination against the child. The work of psychologists in schools is done on a confidential basis, and the best interests of the child are always the top priority. Contact with the parents who have been convicted is permitted where such contact is safe for the child and in accordance with the child's will, in an age-appropriate fashion and in keeping with the child's maturity.

Regarding guardianship of minors. Thank you, Mr. Kesa, for your question. Here what we need to understand when we're talking about minor parents, that there is a mechanism to protect both children, the parent who's a minor and the child born to them. The birth of a child is not a reason to stop education for the minor that is a parent. This parent continues to have the right to study in school or college. Where necessary, the educational process can be adapted, including through an individualized curriculum or under a flexible format provided for by law. At the same time, minor parents have access to information on reproductive and psychological health. We have youth health centers operational in our country and centers that provide psychological support. These issues are also included in the school curriculum, and the youth centres can provide medical, psychological, psychosocial and legal assistance. A question that you raised was on guardianship. According to our legislation, the Code on Marriage and Family, minor parents have the right to live with their child and to participate in bringing them up. At the age of 16, they can exercise parental rights independently. If the minor parent has not yet reached 16, then guardianship shifts and it is exercised by a person from their milieu. It might be an aunt, a grandmother, or an older brother or sister. They have guardianship of the child jointly with the minor parent. Being a minor parent itself is not a reason for separation from the child born to them. There have not been any cases recorded of this in our country. In the case of a family crisis, the guardianship authorities act immediately, as do family support centers. doing their utmost to keep the child in the family environment and for them to have a fully fledged, dignified life. The success of our approach is demonstrated as we focus on the right to continue in education and allowing them to fully exercise their parental responsibilities. Regarding the question on migration status, The Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection. I will answer first. On migration status, in accordance with the legislation of Kazakhstan, migration status is determined by the resident status of the migrant in our country. It was noted that a child should not have to wait for final determination of migration status for education. They are given a temporary refugee certificate, which allows them to access education. All children, refugees and asylum seekers have the right to free of charge primary and secondary education. And so access to education is ensured at the same time as their migration status is being considered. Children with such a status who have not reached 18, number 93 of these, 28 are refugees, rather asylum seekers and 64 refugees. Thank you.

In response to Ms. Yanukovich on children resident in these institutions, I would like to tell you that in Kazakhstan, There are around 120,000 children with disabilities. We have 21 centers to provide specialized social services where children with disabilities are resident and they have nervous system disorders and motor disorders and others. Children are admitted to these organizations where they have orphan status or where they are left without parental care. Before a child reaches the age of 18, under our legislation, the legal representative is the parent who protects their rights and legitimate interests and takes decisions in the best interests of the child. We are steadily developing our system to support the family and providing services to ensure that children with disabilities have the opportunity to remain in the family environment and receive assistance in their home. They receive assistance not only in healthcare institutions, but they are also provided with the opportunity for home study. Now, on social protection of children living in these institutions. To protect the interests of children with disabilities, we have a comprehensive, multi-level approach. The national preventive mechanism is especially important. Its representatives carry out independent monitoring of closed institutions, including ones that are home to children with disabilities.

The main purpose of these.

Visits is to assess the living conditions of the children and to identify any cases of cruel treatment, torture, or any other violations. Thank you very much for Ms. Marabel's questions. Mary Bellof, that is. We would like to say that we need to distinguish three main aspects. First of all, the understanding of deviant behaviour itself. Under our new policy, we... have de facto moved from a stigmatising approach, where the child received the overall status of deviant behaviour. As of 2026, we have a new law on the prevention of offences, and we have introduced a completely different approach, which is pedagogical support for the minor who requires extra attention. pedagogical support is designed as a comprehensive, individualised form of support with social and psychological aspects in order to ensure early detection and timely support for the child. Particularly important to us is the fact that we have expanded not the category of children to whom restrictive measures may be applied, but rather the possibilities for identifying them at an early stage and supporting them through their early stages of development is optimised so as to try and get them back onto the right track. There are also measures in place to address homelessness and neglect among children and for children who have been victims of violence or harsh treatment or bullying and also children who have witnessed violence. It's very important to understand here that this is not a punishment, it's not placing children in the category of offenders and it's not a basis for depriving children of their liberty. Another important aspect is the placement of children in special organisations. Under our new act on the prevention of offences, we have five organisations in our country. They used to be called special organisations for children with defiant behaviour. They have now been renamed, and they are just special educational organisations. There are four of them and one special organization with a secure regime. Special organizations may receive children aged 11 to 18 who have committed administrative offenses on a regular basis, who of their own will leave their family on a repeated basis, who refuse to attend school, or who are showing other antisocial behavior and here it's very important to draw attention to the fact that the purpose of these organizations is not to punish they're not to be perceived as penitentiary establishments or anything these are really organizations that are under the education system and our task is to ensure education and resocialization rehabilitation of children through these organizations in our country we also have one organization which has a special regime, and this one is still under the Ministry of Education, that here the regime is linked to the fact that children have manifested a tendency to criminal offences. but have not yet reached the age of criminal liability, or there are individual cases of deprivation of liberty by a court, or criminal liability, or penalties for offences that have been imposed on the child. But that does not mean that the child is automatically institutionalised. There are two main tracks here, different mechanisms. And the third question you asked is to the legislation, and why is the number of reported offences relatively low, or complaints. The low number of reported offences cannot automatically be interpreted as a low level of violence. We therefore look not only at the criminal statistics, but indeed at the entire detection system that we have put in place in our country. We, over the last two days, have spoken a lot about the 111 contact centres and we've mentioned the fact that over 120,000 complaints or requests were received through the line and many of them were seeking information or consultations. So it's important to distinguish when there is a call for help from a child or where there's a risk that is detected as to there being a potential criminal or administrative offence. These are different indicators. And the fact that there's a call or an appeal does not necessarily mean that there is an offence. We are not trying to artificially lower the number of registered cases, but lowering the latency of violence and ensuring early detection of risks of violence. At a certain stage, we always look at the potential indicators which suggest that our children are becoming more, they're trusting the state more, they're turning to law enforcement bodies and they're actually reporting their problems much more than before. Thank you, Madam Chair. Allow me for the remaining time to respond to the questions from Susan Ahu. that she asked yesterday about equal policy in education and the impact on children belonging to ethnic minorities. In Kazakhstan, the right to receive education in the mother tongue is enshrined in law. In practice, the possibility for tuition in ethnic minority languages is also provided. We have a national database And according to that, 71,000 children are studying in Uzbek, 14,000 in Uyghur, and in Tajik, around 3,000 pupils are studying. Tuition in Uzbek is organized by 108 schools, 62 for Uyghur, and 12 for Tajik language. Moreover, this is about schools as a whole, but also classes that offer tuition in several languages. For children, it is important to study the mother tongue and literature, and this is foreseen by educational curricula. There are textbooks that are provided and other educational material. Linguistic specificities are taken into account when looking at the results, and there are classes with Uzbek, Uyghur, or Tajik students. The students have to sit an exam on their mother language. when they take these courses and the results are harmonised for all children regardless of the language of tuition. So our language policy addresses two challenges in one go, preserving the opportunity for pupils to receive education and to study their mother tongue, ensuring the study of the state language as well and equal access to education. We believe that the language of tuition should not be the factor that determines the educational opportunities for children. It should not be a limiting factor in any way. It is important that children can discover their own culture and language, but also speak the state language and have equal opportunities to receive quality education and to continue language tuition regardless of their ethnic belonging.

we still have five minutes on early marriage a question was asked yesterday in Kazakhstan The general minimum age for marriage for men and women is 18. That is the law. There are exceptions that remain for certain cases. The age of marriage may be reduced by no more than two years and only in two cases. One is pregnancy or the birth of a shared child, with the consent of the minors themselves and their parents and guardians. There are no other grounds for early marriage that are foreseen by law. Historically, this norm came in as a protective mechanism so that early pregnancy or parenthood was not an issue for the health of the mother or the newborn, and also it was to ensure the protection of the right of the newborn to live and grow up in a family. This norm was therefore designed not as a general permission for early marriage, but as a protective mechanism when pregnancy or a shared child are already on the scene. Registering marriages in this case is allowed and is accompanied by additional support. There are mutual obligations that the spouses have to undertake in terms of their property and other family guarantees when entering into marriage. The woman, for instance, or the girl, has the right to keep the child. There is also a standard in place to protect not the marriage but the children involved, so the parents and the newborn, to live in a family environment. We are aware of the standard of 18 years of age without exception for the minimum legal age of marriage, and we are very much in favour of bringing our legislation into line with the convention. So, we are open to looking at whether we could provide the protections that are currently provided for through this exception without actually having that exception. We are looking at other ways to ensure that we can protect children aged under 18 from entering into marriage.
